claims.text: The baseline TiVNbTa alloy is a single-phase, dendritic BCC material.
Baseline TiVNbTa has a lower-temperature yield strength of approximately 800 MPa.
The yield strength of baseline TiVNbTa decreases to approximately 330 MPa at 1273 K.
Baseline TiVNbTa has a compressive strength of approximately 423 MPa at 1273 K.
Forging TiVNbTa at approximately 1000–1100 K will cause plastic deformation and dislocation multiplication.
A brief anneal at approximately 900 K will stabilize and lock in the forging-induced dislocation substructures.
The forging-and-annealing treatment will produce a high density of stable dislocation substructures and refined subgrain boundaries in TiVNbTa.
The brief anneal will preserve the refined structure without significant grain coarsening.
At elevated temperature, deformation can transition from screw-dislocation control to edge-dislocation control.
The proposed thermomechanical treatment will promote the transition from screw-dislocation-controlled slip to edge-dislocation-controlled slip in TiVNbTa.
A stable dislocation network will impede dislocation glide and climb at high temperature.
Edge-dislocation-controlled deformation is associated with high-temperature strength or a strength plateau in refractory high-entropy alloys.
The stabilized dislocation structure and edge-dislocation-controlled mechanism will mitigate the loss of TiVNbTa yield strength at 1273 K.
After treatment, TiVNbTa yield strength at 1273 K will increase from approximately 330 MPa toward 400–500 MPa.
The treatment will maintain or improve compressive performance relative to conventionally cast TiVNbTa.
The intervention is applicable over approximately 300–1273 K and at compressive stresses up to about 500 MPa.
The treated TiVNbTa is suitable as an intermediate heat-transfer layer between tungsten and CuCrZr.
A hydrothermally processed TiVNb alloy retains approximately 405 MPa strength at 800 °C, showing that weak temperature dependence of strength can occur in a related Ti-V-Nb alloy.
Annealed T0.1 and T0.2 alloys resist softening at 600–800 °C but soften significantly at 1000 °C.
Failure to obtain a statistically significant improvement greater than about 15–20% in 1273 K yield strength, or failure to observe the proposed stabilized substructure, will falsify the hypothesis.
